sections.heading: Teach me to pray honestly
sections.text:
Father, you hear prayer, and I need you to teach me how to pray.

I admit that my mouth and my heart have not always been saying the same thing. I have spoken your name lightly, when even heaven speaks it with reverence. I have asked for things that would have harmed me if you had given them. I have treated some of your best gifts as if they were small. I have been wrong in what I hoped for and wrong in what I feared.

I am not wise enough to choose my own way. I cannot safely steer my own life without you.
theological_themes: God hears the prayers of his people.
True prayer requires honesty before God, not religious words disconnected from the heart.
Human beings are not competent to direct their lives apart from God’s wisdom.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm addresses God as the one who hears prayer, which grounds the opening confidence that coming to him is not pointless or unheard.
Jeremiah confesses that people do not have the ability to direct their own steps rightly. That supports the prayer’s admission that self-guidance is unsafe without God.
Jesus warns against honoring God with words while the heart is far from him. This directly illuminates the confession that religious speech can become detached from real devotion.

sections.heading: Let your Spirit shape what I want
sections.text:
Holy Spirit, help me in my weakness. I often do not even know what I should ask for.

Please form better desires in me. Teach me to want what is wise, good, and pleasing to you. Then let my prayers rise out of those desires, so that I am not just asking loudly, but asking rightly, with trust that you hear me.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit helps believers in the weakness and confusion of prayer.
Right desires are not self-produced; they are formed by God’s work in the heart.
Confidence in prayer is tied to asking according to God’s will.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the Spirit helps believers when they do not know how to pray as they ought. This is the clearest biblical basis for asking the Spirit to guide both the content and posture of prayer.
John connects confidence in being heard with asking according to God’s will. The prayer’s desire for ‘right’ asking follows that logic rather than treating prayer as a way to control God.

sections.heading: Help me hold earthly needs loosely
sections.text:
Father, when I ask for ordinary needs and earthly blessings, keep me from clinging to them as if I know best.

I want to bring my needs to you honestly, but I also want to leave them in your hands. You know what I need before I ask. Give what is truly good. Withhold what would pull me away from you. Teach me to trust your fatherly care more than my own judgment.
theological_themes: Temporal blessings may be requested, but they must be submitted to God’s wise fatherly care.
God knows the needs of his children before they ask.
Prayer is not manipulation but trusting dependence.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that the Father knows his children’s needs before they ask. This supports praying for needs without anxious insistence or the assumption that God must be informed or persuaded like a reluctant giver.
Jesus presents the Father as wiser and better than earthly parents in giving good gifts. That grounds the prayer’s trust that God may give or withhold according to loving wisdom.
James warns that prayers can be corrupted by disordered desires. This supports the request not to demand temporal blessings in ways that would serve selfishness or spiritual harm.

sections.heading: Teach me what real prosperity is
sections.text:
Do not let me think I am doing well if my soul is withering.

Do not let me call myself rich if I am poor toward you. Do not let me think I am wise if I am not wise about salvation. Train me to seek your kingdom first, and to measure everything in the light of eternity.

Make my life with you my greatest concern—not as a way to neglect ordinary responsibilities, but because nothing else can matter rightly unless you are first.
theological_themes: True prosperity is spiritual before it is material.
Riches, wisdom, and success are deceptive if they are not ordered toward God.
The kingdom of God must have first place in the believer’s desires.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus tells of a man who had abundance but was not rich toward God. This directly supports the prayer’s refusal to define wealth by possessions rather than by one’s standing before God.
Jesus commands his disciples to seek first God’s kingdom and righteousness. This anchors the prayer’s request for rightly ordered priorities.

Paul says the Scriptures are able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ. This supports the prayer’s distinction between ordinary cleverness and the wisdom that actually matters before God.

sections.heading: Make your blessing worth more to me than success
sections.text:
Lord, if it comes to this, let me be poor, afflicted, overlooked, and still have your blessing, rather than succeed, have everything I want, and be admired while slowly forgetting you.

Keep me from being fooled by the world’s glitter. So much of what looks solid fades like a dream, disappoints like a lie, and leaves the heart restless. Do not let me build my happiness there.

Let my deepest happiness be in your favor, in being made more like you, in living near you, and in serving you. And when my work here is finished, let me gladly come home to be with Christ.
theological_themes: God’s blessing is better than comfort, success, wealth, or human praise.
The world cannot provide lasting satisfaction and must be viewed in light of eternity.
The believer’s deepest joy is found in God’s favor, presence, likeness, and service.
Christian longing to depart this world is a longing to be with Christ, not contempt for God’s good creation or rejection of earthly duties.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that gaining the whole world is worthless if the soul is lost. This strongly supports preferring God’s blessing over success, admiration, or abundance that would lead away from him.
Ecclesiastes describes the emptiness of pleasure and achievement when treated as ultimate. This illuminates the prayer’s language about the world’s vanity and its inability to satisfy the heart.
The psalm locates fullness of joy in God’s presence. That grounds the prayer’s final movement toward happiness in God himself rather than in circumstances.

Paul expresses a desire to depart and be with Christ while still recognizing fruitful labor in this life. This helps frame the prayer’s longing to leave the world as a Christ-centered hope, not escapism.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about desiring to depart from the world could be misunderstood in a modern setting as a desire for death or as contempt for created life. I rendered it as a Pauline longing to be with Christ when one’s earthly work is finished, while preserving the original’s strong detachment from worldly vanity.

The prayer’s willingness to be poor, afflicted, and despised rather than spiritually harmed by success is stark. I preserved that force, but phrased it conditionally so it remains a surrender to God’s blessing rather than a romanticizing of suffering.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted ‘teach me to pray’ not mainly as learning technique, but as asking God to make the heart truthful, reverent, and rightly ordered before him.
I treated ‘wise desires’ as desires shaped by the Holy Spirit and aligned with God’s will, drawing especially on Romans 8 and 1 John 5.
I rendered ‘temporal blessings’ as ordinary needs and earthly blessings, keeping the original distinction between asking for them and demanding them.
I interpreted ‘thy favour, image, presence, service’ as God’s approval and love, conformity to his character, nearness to him, and a life spent serving him.
